core.text: To say *when* something happens, Latin uses a bare ablative with no preposition: **the ablative (the 'at / in (a time)' form)**. *Nocte sōl nōn lūcet* — at night the sun does not shine; *hōrā sextā* — at the sixth hour; *mēnse Iūniō* — in June; *eō tempore* — at that time; *hieme, aestāte, vēre* — in winter, in summer, in spring. The time word simply takes its ablative ending, and English supplies *at, in* or *on*. Latin name: ablātīvus temporis.
English needs a preposition for time — *at night, in June, on Monday*. Latin drops it and lets the ending do the work, just as it drops *with* in *gladiō pugnat* (fights with a sword).
A time word in the ablative, without a preposition, answers 'when?'

invented.en: In winter the boys stay at home.

core.text: The same case says where and when. *In hortō* (in the garden) keeps *in*; *nocte* (at night) has nothing. Place usually keeps the preposition, time usually drops it. So a bare ablative of a time word — *nocte, diē, hōrā, annō, mēnse, tempore, hieme* — is time; a bare ablative of a place word is rare in prose (towns and *domī* apart).

more.text: How long something lasts is the accusative (the object form), not the ablative: *trēs hōrās dormit* — he sleeps for three hours; *multōs annōs* — for many years. Within how long is the ablative again: *tribus diēbus* — within three days. *Paucīs diēbus* can mean either 'within' or 'a few days later' by context.

The learner's notes (week 13): a fourth use of the ablative after place, origin and means, answering *when?* or *at what time?*; Classical Latin has no preposition (*nocte hominēs dormiunt*, *diē hominēs operantur*), but medieval Latin often writes *in autumnō*, *sub nocte*. Use the classical way in composition; expect *in* in later readings.

Ørberg (chapter XIII) uses it throughout the calendar chapter: *mēnse Iūniō diēs longī sunt*, *diēbus prīmīs mēnsium*, *hōrā sextā vel merīdiē*, *nocte*. A&G §423: set phrases behave the same — *initiō* (at the beginning), *fīne* (at the end), *tempore* (in time), *bellō* (in the war).
